h: Who was the Lord of Provan anyway?
p: The name sounds grand, but there's a simple story behind it. The house became linked with the canon who held the prebend of Barlanark, a church post whose holder was known as the Lord of Provan. He's thought to have used the house as his town lodging when he was in Glasgow on cathedral business. The name stuck long after the job disappeared.

Spare a few minutes for St Nicholas Garden out the back. It's laid out as a physic garden, the kind of herb garden that supplied medicines in medieval times, which ties in nicely with the house's origins as part of a hospital. Look out too for the Tontine Faces, a set of carved stone heads that once decorated the old Tontine building in the city and now gaze out across the garden. They've got real character and make a great photo.

This is a quick visit: most people see it all in under an hour, which makes it ideal for slotting into a busier day. It's great for short attention spans and for anyone who likes to tick off a few sights in one area.

Glasgow Cathedral, across the street, came through the Reformation in far better shape than most medieval Scottish churches, and its lower church, where St Mungo's tomb lies, is atmospheric. From there, head down the High Street towards the Merchant City for food and drink, or carry on to Glasgow Green and the People's Palace for a peek at the city's social history.
